393.title: The quail and the hawk
393.hook: a quail safe in its own field is caught when it strays (SN 47.6)
393.howItsDone: In many Buddhist communities, mindfulness is described as a practitioner's own ground or home base, returned to through the day; monastics often keep simple routines and guard the senses when they go into town as a way of staying in that range.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six animals, and your line, the post holds. When something dragged your attention away, did you feel your feet first? Day three hundred ninety-three.

A hawk drops out of the sky and comes up with a quail in its claws. And the quail, being carried off, starts talking. Not begging. Scolding itself. This is my own fault, it says. I wandered out of my own range into somebody else's. If I'd stayed in my home ground, the ground my mother and father knew, this hawk would be no match for me. The hawk, apparently amused, asks: and where is this home ground of yours? A plowed field, says the quail, covered with clods of earth. Today: the quail and the hawk.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE HAWK'S CLAWS.` → `I LEFT MY OWN GROUND.` → `A PLOWED FIELD, FULL OF CLODS.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.6, in the Connected Discourses on mindfulness. The hawk, proud of its strength, lets the quail go. Fine, it says. Go home. Even there you won't escape me. The quail flies back to its plowed field, climbs onto a big clod of earth, and calls up: come and get me now, hawk. The hawk folds its wings and dives at full speed. The quail watches it come, and at the last moment slips down behind the clod. The hawk hits the earth breast first. Then the Buddha explains. Don't wander outside your own range, monks, into the range of others. In others' ground, Mara, the tempter, gets his chance. What isn't your range? The five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at desire. And what is your own range, the ground your fathers knew? The four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience. Two things stand out. First, the quail isn't stronger than the hawk. It simply knows its ground: every furrow, every clod. Safety in this story isn't power. It's familiarity. Second, the word the text uses for range is gocara, the word for a pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows by heart. Mindfulness, in this picture, isn't a fortress you build. It's a field you know so well you can disappear into it. And the hawk doesn't stop being a hawk. The quail still lives in a world with hawks in it. What changes is where it's standing when one comes.
screen: `THE HAWK LETS THE QUAIL GO.` · `A CLOD IN A PLOWED FIELD.` · `YOUR RANGE: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · `GOCARA — A PASTURE KNOWN BY HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN GROUND.`

segments.voice: For this sit, your field is small: the breath and the body sitting. Get to know its clods. Where does the breath touch first, at the nostrils or in the chest? Where is the body heavy? When a thought flies off toward someone else's field, a plan, a worry, a screen, notice the moment you've left. Then come back to a clod you know: one breath, one point of contact. Nothing to fight. Just home ground. The bell holds the time.
The quail and the hawk. Safety isn't strength; it's staying in your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE HAWK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: your own ground. Today, when you feel yourself drifting somewhere you didn't mean to go, name one thing right in front of you, and stand there. Day three hundred ninety-three.

screen: `DAY 393 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MONKEY AND THE PITCH.`

394.title: The monkey and the pitch
394.hook: a monkey caught in a hunter's sticky pitch by grabbing with every limb (SN 47.7)
394.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use this simile to describe how grasping compounds itself; many practitioners work with it by pausing to notice an urge before acting on it, in meditation and in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quail and the hawk, and your line, your own ground. When you drifted, did naming one thing in front of you bring you home? Day three hundred ninety-four.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE HAWK — YOUR OWN GROUND.`

segments.voice: Hunters in the old Himalaya had a trick for catching monkeys. No net. No arrow. Just a smear of sticky pitch along the trails where monkeys travel. A wise monkey sees it and keeps going. A curious one touches it with one paw. Stuck. So it does what anyone would do: it uses the other paw to pull the first one free. Stuck. Then a foot. Then the other foot. Then, out of ideas, it tries its mouth. Today: the monkey and the pitch, the last of this stretch's pictures of mindfulness.
screen: `PITCH ON THE MONKEY TRAIL.` → `ONE PAW. THEN THE OTHER.` → `THEN THE FEET. THEN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.7, right next to the quail. The Buddha describes three kinds of mountain country. Rugged places where neither monkeys nor people go. Places where monkeys go but people don't. And even, pleasant places where both go. In that third kind of place, hunters lay pitch along the trails. The foolish monkey, stuck at five points, lies there crying out, and the hunter picks it up and goes off with it. The lesson is the same as the quail's: keep to your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness. The range of others is the five cords of sense pleasure. But this picture adds something the quail story didn't. The quail story is about where you are. The monkey story is about how you get stuck: by trying to get unstuck the same way you got stuck. Every limb that grabs to free the first gets caught too. You've seen it. An argument you try to win with one more message. A craving you try to settle with one more taste. A worry you try to think your way out of, by thinking more. The pitch is laid where life is pleasant; that's the point of putting it there. And grabbing is the reflex. Mindfulness, here, is the pause before the second paw: seeing the pitch as pitch. The text doesn't call the monkey wicked or the forest evil. The wise monkey sees the pitch and walks around it. That's all. And this closes six days on right mindfulness: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, the six animals and their post, the quail's own ground, and the monkey. Six pictures for one factor of the path.

segments.voice: In this sit, look for one sticky place. It might be a thought you keep returning to, a sound you keep resisting, or a plan for later you can't put down. When you find it, notice the second paw: the urge to fix it, push it away, settle it right now. Don't grab. Let your hands rest open on your knees, literally, and just watch the pull. It may stay. That's fine. You're only learning where the pitch is. The bell holds the time.
The monkey and the pitch. The trap that holds you tighter the more you grab to get free.
screen: `THE MONKEY AND THE PITCH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: don't grab the pitch. Today, when something sticks, a message, a craving, a worry, wait one breath before the second grab. Day three hundred ninety-four.

395.title: Right concentration
395.hook: the mind gathered and unified, in the four jhanas (MN 141)
395.howItsDone: Buddhists across schools train concentration in meditation, often on the breath; in Theravada communities it is commonly taught as calm (samatha) alongside insight (vipassana), and Zen and Tibetan schools have their own methods for steadying the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the monkey and the pitch, and your line, don't grab the pitch. Did you catch one second grab before it happened? Day three hundred ninety-five, and the last factor of the path.
screen: `THE MONKEY AND THE PITCH — DON'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: Sunlight falling on a sheet of paper does nothing much. Gather the same sunlight through a magnifying glass, and the paper starts to smoke. Nothing was added. No extra sun. The light was only collected into one point. Water from a garden hose works the same way: spread into a mist, it barely wets the grass; gathered into a stream, it reaches the far end of the yard. The eighth and last factor of the eightfold path is about that kind of gathering. Today: right concentration.
screen: `THE SAME SUNLIGHT.` → `GATHERED INTO ONE POINT.` → `NOTHING ADDED.`

segments.voice: In Pali it's samma samadhi. Samadhi comes from a verb meaning to put together, to collect. The mind gathered. In MN 141, where Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, right concentration is defined simply: the four jhanas, four deepening states of meditative absorption. We'll spend the next four days on them, one at a time, with the Buddha's own pictures for each. Today is about the gathering itself, and three things are worth knowing. First, concentration in the Buddha's teaching isn't a strain. It isn't frowning hard at a point. In the suttas, the gathered mind is described again and again as pleasant, even joyful. Second, it's never alone. MN 117 calls it noble right concentration with its supports: the seven factors that come before it. A mind gathered to plan a burglary is gathered, too. It isn't right concentration. Third, concentration and understanding work as partners. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's translation: “Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.” Buddhist schools differ on how much concentration a person needs, and how deep. In Theravada teaching, many describe calm, samatha, and insight, vipassana, developed together; some teachers stress deep absorption, others a lighter, moment-to-moment steadiness. Zen and Tibetan schools train the gathered mind in their own ways. Across them, the basic point holds: a scattered mind has trouble seeing clearly, and a gathered one sees more.
screen: `SAMADHI — THE MIND GATHERED.` · `NOT A STRAIN, AND NEVER ALONE.` · `KNOWLEDGE AND MEDITATION TOGETHER.` · `SCHOOLS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `GATHERED.`

segments.voice: The outline suggests ten minutes on the breath. The bell holds two; if you have more time, keep going when it rings. Choose one place where the breath is clearest, the nostrils or the belly, and let your attention rest there. When it scatters, and it will, gather it back gently, the way you'd sweep crumbs into your hand. No need to count the scatterings. Every gathering is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Samadhi. Concentration: the mind gathered and unified, the eighth factor of the path.
Your line: gathered. Once today, do one thing with your whole attention, the dishes, a conversation, a short walk, and notice what changes. Day three hundred ninety-five.

396.title: The first jhana
396.hook: like bath powder kneaded with water until it is soaked through: joy filling the body (MN 39)
396.howItsDone: Jhana practice is taught especially in Theravada meditation lineages, usually with a teacher and often on retreat; Chan and Zen take their names from the same word, dhyana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadhi, and your line, gathered. Did you do one thing with your whole attention, and did anything change? Day three hundred ninety-six.

A boy sits in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father is busy with the work of the day. Nobody is watching him. And something happens: his mind goes quiet and bright, and his body fills with a gentle joy. Years later, after six years of starving himself and pushing harder than almost anyone ever has, that grown man remembers the afternoon under the tree, and wonders: could that be the way to awakening? Today: the first jhana.
screen: `UNDER THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `QUIET, BRIGHT, GLAD.` → `COULD THAT BE THE WAY?`

segments.voice: The man is the Buddha-to-be, and he tells this story himself, in MN 36. He'd been wary of that kind of pleasure, he says; then he saw he didn't need to fear it, because it had nothing to do with sense pleasures. Jhana is the Pali word. In Sanskrit it's dhyana, the same word that traveled to China as chan and to Japan as zen. It means meditative absorption. In MN 39 the Buddha describes the first one: quite secluded from sense pleasures and unwholesome states, a person enters the first jhana, with directed and sustained thought, and with joy and pleasure born of that seclusion. Then he gives a picture from a world before bars of soap. A skilled bath attendant pours bath powder into a metal bowl, sprinkles it with water, bit by bit, and kneads it into a ball, until the moisture soaks every grain, inside and out, yet doesn't drip. That's how this joy fills the body. Look at the picture closely. The joy is physical: the text says it drenches and fills the whole body. It's thorough: no part is left dry. It's contained: nothing leaks. And there's still a hand at work. Thinking is still present in the first jhana, directed and sustained, like the attendant's hands working the powder. The later jhanas let even that settle. One honest note: teachers today disagree about how deep this state is. Some describe a rare, total absorption; others a calmer, more accessible steadiness. The texts give pictures, not a depth gauge.
screen: `JHANA, DHYANA, CHAN, ZEN.` · `SECLUDED, YET STILL THINKING.` · `BATH POWDER SOAKED THROUGH.` · `TEACHERS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `SOAKED THROUGH.`

segments.voice: No need to reach for joy. Just look for any ease in the body that's already here. Maybe the hands are warm. Maybe the shoulders let go a little on the out-breath. Maybe the belly is soft. Find one small place of ease, and see whether it can spread, slowly, like water into powder, one grain at a time. If you find nothing, that's honest too: rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Jhana. Meditative absorption. In the first, joy born of seclusion soaks the whole body, like water kneaded into bath powder.
Your line: soaked through. Once today, when something feels good, a warm cup, sun on your face, let it soak in for three breaths before you move on. Day three hundred ninety-six.

fork.reveal: he saw that this joy had nothing to do with sense pleasures, so there was no need to fear it, and he took it as a path.

original.note: Pali jhāna: meditative absorption; Sanskrit dhyāna (ध्यान), which became Chinese chan and Japanese zen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trance where the world disappears.
what it means: a gathered absorption that, in the first jhana, still has thought, and soaks the body with joy.

397.title: The second jhana
397.hook: a lake fed by a spring from within (MN 39)
397.howItsDone: Meditators who train in the jhanas usually do so under a teacher's guidance, often on retreat; many Buddhists also use the phrase 'noble silence' for periods of silence kept at retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jhana, and your line, soaked through. Did one good moment get three whole breaths to soak in? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Some lakes are filled by rivers: water pours down from the hills, and if the rivers dry up, the lake shrinks. Some are topped up by rain. And some, the rare ones, are filled from beneath. A cold spring wells up from the lakebed, and the lake stays full even in a dry season. You can't see where the water is coming from. It just keeps arriving. Today: the second jhana, and the inner spring.
screen: `FED BY RIVERS.` → `FED BY RAIN.` → `FED FROM BENEATH.`

segments.voice: In MN 39 the Buddha describes the next stage. With the stilling of directed and sustained thought, a person enters the second jhana: inner stillness, the mind become one, without directed or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration. Then his picture. A lake whose waters well up from below. No stream flows in from the east, the west, the north or the south. The sky doesn't fill it with rain from time to time. But a cool spring wells up within it and soaks the whole lake, so that no part of it is left untouched. Set it beside yesterday's picture. In the first jhana, water had to be added by a hand, sprinkled and kneaded into the powder. The joy was born of seclusion, of stepping away. Here the hand is gone. Thinking has gone quiet. And the joy is born of concentration itself; it rises from inside. Two Pali words carry this. Sampasadana: inner clearness, or inner confidence, like muddy water settling until you can see the bottom. And ekodibhava: the mind becoming single, unified. The calm doesn't depend on anything outside: no good news, no compliment, no perfect weather. The texts give this stage a lovely name, too. In SN 21.1, Moggallana is taught that the second jhana is what's called noble silence. Not the silence of a closed mouth, but of a mind that has stopped talking to itself.
screen: `THINKING GROWS STILL.` · `A LAKE FED FROM WITHIN.` · `NO RIVER, NO RAIN.` · `NOBLE SILENCE.` · then, large: `THE INNER SPRING.`

segments.voice: Don't go looking for calm out there. Sit, let the breath settle, and when a thought comes, let it pass without picking it up. Between thoughts there may be small gaps: a breath or two with nothing to do. Rest in one of those gaps, and notice whether anything wells up on its own: quiet, coolness, a little gladness. If nothing does, the gap itself is enough. The bell holds the time.
The second jhana. Thinking grows still, and joy wells up from within, like a lake fed by its own spring.
Your line: the inner spring. Today, when you reach for something outside to feel better, pause for one breath and check whether something quieter is already there. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

a name for the second jhana

that stilling is what marks the move from the first.
the lake in the simile is kept full by rain

fork.reveal: the spring rises from inside and soaks the whole lake. the calm of the second jhana needs nothing poured in from outside.

original.note: Pali sampasādana: inner clearness or confidence, like water settling clear; a quality of the second jhāna.

trapdoor: what you thought: a deeper level of the same thing.
what it means: thinking grows still, and calm and joy rise from within, needing nothing added.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the spring-fed lake)

398.title: The third jhana
398.hook: lotuses under water, soaked from root to tip (MN 39)
398.howItsDone: In Theravada meditation teaching the jhanas are usually described in this order, with the fading of rapture and the growth of equanimity marking the third; the lotus is a common Buddhist image in art and teaching across schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the second jhana, and your line, the inner spring. Before you reached for something outside, did you find anything quieter already there? Day three hundred ninety-eight.

In a lotus pond, most of the flowers rise up and open on the surface, where everyone can see them. Those are the ones on the postcards. But some never come up. They sprout under water, grow under water, and stay there, cool water all around them from the roots to the tips of the petals. You'd walk right past them. Nothing about them is showy. They're thriving anyway. Today: the third jhana, and the lotus under water.

Here is how MN 39 describes the third jhana. With the fading away of joy, a person abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, and enters the third jhana, of which the noble ones say: one who is equanimous and mindful dwells in pleasure. Then the picture. In a pond of blue, red or white lotuses, some are born and grow in the water and thrive immersed, never rising out, and cool water soaks them from their tips to their roots. That is how this quiet pleasure fills the body. What changes from yesterday? Two Pali words help. Piti is joy with a bubble in it: rapture, excitement, the child on the morning of a trip. Sukha is pleasure without the bubble: contentment, the grandmother on the porch. In the third jhana, piti fades and sukha stays. And a new quality comes forward: upekkha, equanimity, looking on evenly. Many centuries later, the Visuddhimagga, a Theravada meditation manual, gives an image for the difference. A traveler worn out in the desert hears that there's a pond at the edge of a wood: that thrill is piti. Then he reaches it, drinks and rests in the shade: that's sukha. The lotus doesn't need to rise to the surface to be fully alive. The third jhana is happiness that no longer needs to rise and be seen: the mind stays mindful and fully aware, and the ease simply soaks through.
screen: `THE JOY FADES; THE EASE STAYS.` · `PITI, BUBBLING; SUKHA, CONTENT.` · `HEARING OF WATER, THEN DRINKING.` · `LOTUSES SOAKED, ROOT TO TIP.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS UNDER WATER.`

segments.voice: This time, don't look for anything bright. Let the breath be ordinary. Notice the body sitting, and whether there's any plain, quiet okayness in it: not excitement, just enough. If thoughts come, let them pass like ripples on the surface overhead, while you stay below, cool and still. The bell holds the time.
The third jhana. The bubbling joy fades and a quiet, mindful ease remains, like a lotus soaked in cool water from root to tip.
Your line: the lotus under water. Today, let one good moment stay quiet: enjoy it without posting it, telling anyone, or even naming it. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

options: nothing: the meditation is over

what it means: the bubbling joy fades and a quieter ease remains, mindful and even.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the lotus pond simile)

399.title: The fourth jhana
399.hook: a person wrapped head to foot in clean white cloth (MN 39)
399.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the fourth jhana is often described as the basis for insight and the higher knowledges; meditators who work with the jhanas usually do so under a teacher, and many Buddhists recall that the Buddha's awakening and final passing are both told with the fourth jhana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the third jhana, and your line, the lotus under water. Did one good moment stay quiet, unposted and untold? Day three hundred ninety-nine, the end of the week.
screen: `THE THIRD JHANA — THE LOTUS UNDER WATER.`

segments.voice: A clean white cloth, fresh off the line, still cool. Someone sits down, and the cloth is drawn over them from the top of the head to the soles of the feet. Not to hide them. Just to cover them evenly, all the way around. No part warmer than another. No part left out. It's a strange, simple picture, almost nothing happening in it, and that's the point. It's the last of the Buddha's four pictures of deep concentration. Today: the fourth jhana.
screen: `A CLEAN WHITE CLOTH.` → `HEAD TO FOOT, EVENLY.` → `NOTHING LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: MN 39 describes it like this. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the earlier fading of gladness and sorrow, a person enters the fourth jhana: neither painful nor pleasant, with mindfulness made pure by equanimity. They sit pervading the body with a pure, bright mind, the way a person sits wrapped from the head down in white cloth, so that no part of the body isn't covered. Look at the path the four jhanas trace. First, thinking settles. Then the bubbling joy fades. Now even pleasure is let go. Each stage is less, not more. What's left is equanimity and pure mindfulness, like the plain white cloth: no pattern, no color, nothing to grab. Strangely, the suttas treat this not as an ending but as a platform. In MN 36, the Buddha says that on the night of his awakening, with his mind concentrated like this, pure and bright, steady and pliable, he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges followed. And in the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana, DN 16, his last moments pass through the jhanas, and he passes away on emerging from the fourth. So the week ends here: the monkey and the pitch, then right concentration and its four pictures: bath powder soaked through, a lake fed by a spring, lotuses under water, and a person wrapped in white. Four pictures, each quieter than the last.

segments.voice: Sit, and let your attention cover the body evenly, head to foot, the way the cloth covers. No spot more interesting than another. Not chasing a pleasant feeling, not pushing away an unpleasant one. If something itches, it can itch. If something is pleasant, it can be pleasant. Rest in the middle, still, and let it all be covered by plain, clear knowing. The bell holds the time.
The fourth jhana. Neither pleasure nor pain, only equanimity and pure mindfulness, covering the whole body like clean white cloth.
Your line: wrapped in white. Today, meet one pleasant moment and one unpleasant moment with the same even attention, and notice how that feels. Day three hundred ninety-nine.
